# Introduction

## The reversal of educational difference


Women born just after the Second World War were less likely than men of the same cohort to hold a degree. For every subsequent cohort, the gap has narrowed and reversed across most European countries, including Austria.

::: {#fig-tertiary-difference}
{{< include build/figures/tertiary_difference.qmd >}}
**The female educational advantage by cohort.**\
The measure and most of the design follow Erát [@erat2021], but the data include more countries (30) and survey rounds.\
*Source:* own calculations based on the rounds 1-11 of the European Social Survey[@europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2012; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2018; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023a; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2025; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2025a; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023b; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023c; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2026; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2025b; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2026a].

:::

The reversal in @fig-tertiary-difference is an aggregation of individuals by sex, women's degree share in each cohort against men's. Individuals, however, pair, and a change in the education propagates into the educational composition of the couples. Education is both a strong social signal and a stratifying force [@kalmijn1998]. Consequently, how couples form is rarely random.

Educational assortative mating describes the non-random pattern of individuals selecting partners based on education level^[There are two types of assortative mating: positive and negative (also called disassortative), in which partners are similar and dissimilar to each other, respectively. In this thesis, for brevity, assortative mating means the positive kind.]. The sorting's consequences extend beyond the couples themselves, from the socioeconomic status of the household to the life chances of their children. Between households, sorting on education is responsible for a significant share of cross-sectional income inequality^[Nevertheless, changes in sorting over time were not associated with the changes in household income inequality.] [@eika2019]. Within the household, both genders were shown to have lower well-being when man is more educated in the partnership [@wang2025]. Across generations, sorting both reinforces educational reproduction, as resources are concentrated on the children of educated parents, and reduces it since those parents tend to have fewer children [@wittemann2024].

The change in educational composition is accompanied by the shifts in the share of hypogamous, homogamous and hypergamous couples.^[A couple is hypogamous when the woman holds more education than the man, homogamous when they hold the same and hypergamous when the man holds more education than the woman (see @fig-mating-terms below for how the three terms relate to disassortative and assortative mating).] Hypogamy is more common in the countries where women hold more education than men, which is a well-recorded finding globally [@esteve2012; @esteve2016]. In most European countries hypogamous couples now outnumber hypergamous ones [@dehauw2017; @wang2025].  By contrast, homogamy shows no common trend across countries, time and metrics [@katrnak2020; @hirschl2024]. Whether hypergamy is in decline is contested [@urbina2024].

::: {#fig-mating-terms .column-margin}
{{< include build/figures/mating_terms.qmd >}}
**The correspondence of the terms: hypo-, homo- and hypergamy with disassortative and assortative mating.**\
The height of the curve is the distance in education between partners, and thus hypogamy and hypergamy lie on the disassortative side, opposite to homogamy on the assortative one.
:::


How couples are operationalized affects the measurements of educational composition. In this thesis, the couples are defined narrowly — parents whose first children^[Per Austrian registry of births. More on the data used in the [Data chapter](#sec-data).] were born in Austria within the period of 1990-2007. Therefore, the research is scoped accordingly — the results are not to be generalized to the total population. Nevertheless, for illustrative purposes and to embed the analysis in the broader context, the thesis is not limited to the discussion of the narrow definition of couples and broader trends are considered.

Assortative mating describes outcomes, not what drives them. To what extent does the rise of hypogamy follow mechanically from the increase in the number of educated women, and to what extent from the changed partner preferences? In other words, how to distinguish the effect of the changes in the *margins* of the table from the changes in the *association* between partners' characteristics? @fig-couples-shares is two such tables for the data used in the thesis. The education range runs from at most compulsory schooling through apprenticeship and Matura^[Latin word used as a name for the secondary school exit exam. The noun is capitalized as in German and left untranslated to indicate the specifics of Austrian educational system.] to a tertiary degree. The most evident change is the reduction in the share of couples where both partners had attained "apprenticeship" as the highest degree. Overall, the values have shifted towards higher education for both sexes. 

::: {#fig-couples-shares .wideblock}
{{< include build/figures/couples_shares.qmd >}}
**The shares of couples by educational composition in 1990 and 2007, with the margins.**\
For each panel, the sum of tiles is equal to 100% (there may be variations due to rounding). Each margin is a sum of the respective row or column. The total counts for the panels are 1,472 couples in 1990 and 1,605 in 2007.\
*Source:* own calculations based on the Austrian register data on first births.
:::

Association can be defined in more than one way. Following [@leesch2025], @fig-decomposition operationalizes it as the odds ratios of the tables and separates margins from association by applying iterative proportional fitting,^[Table $A$ is fitted to the margins of table $B$ while preserving the odds ratios between any two rows and two columns. Each iteration alternately rescales rows and columns until convergence to a unique table [@fienberg1970].] By holding the association from either year fixed, two counterfactual tables are obtained. In both cases the margins account for most of the rise in hypogamy: fixing the 1990 association reproduces ~72% of the increase, and fixing the 2007 association reproduces ~82%.

::: {#fig-decomposition .wideblock}
{{< include build/figures/decomposition.qmd >}}
**Educational decomposition as two paths from 1990 to 2007.**\
Tables along each row share association and tables along each column share margins. The observed tables (same ones as in @fig-couples-shares) occupy the main diagonal, 1990 in the upper left and 2007 in the lower right. Each table shows a share of hypogamous couples in the upper left, which is the sum of the respective highlighted area. Each arrow holds one component fixed while changing the other, and its label indicates the change in the share of hypogamous couples (in percentage points). The path above the main diagonal of the figure adjusts the margins first and then the association. The other path does the reverse, adjusting association first and then the margins.\
*Source:* own calculations based on the Austrian register data on first births.
:::
